note: DRAFT v1 module checks and final designation exam for the CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner course. Original CARSI questions for Australian and New Zealand conditions; no IICRC standard text reproduced. Answer positions balanced. SME review and sign-off required before seeding.

quizzes.title: CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner — Module 1 check

questions.questionText: You arrive at a wet house. Which comes first in the CARSI drying arc?
options: Set up air movers across the wet floor
Take the final dry readings
Assess the job and make it safe
Send the owner a drying invoice
questions.explanation: Assess and make safe comes first: power to wet areas is isolated and hazards are identified before any equipment goes in or any reading is trusted.

questions.questionText: Who holds the primary duty of care for workers on a drying job in both Australia and New Zealand?
options: The person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU)
The homeowner whose house is wet
The insurer who assigned the job
The equipment hire company
questions.explanation: Both the model WHS laws and the NZ Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 place the primary duty on the PCBU, so far as is reasonably practicable.

questions.questionText: A 1996 house in Auckland needs plasterboard cut along a flood line. What should happen first?
options: Cut it, because only pre-1990 buildings can contain asbestos
Cut it wet, because wet asbestos is always safe
Ask the owner whether they think it has asbestos
Treat it as possibly containing asbestos and arrange sampling before cutting
questions.explanation: WorkSafe New Zealand advises that any building built or renovated before 2000 could contain asbestos, and you cannot tell by looking. Sample before you cut.

questions.questionText: Which reading makes a valid dry standard for a wet hallway timber floor?
options: A plasterboard wall in the same hallway
The same timber floor in an unaffected bedroom, same meter, same scale
A number remembered from a job last summer
The wet hallway floor read on a different meter
questions.explanation: A dry standard comes from the same material in an unaffected part of the same building, measured with the same meter on the same scale.

questions.questionText: Why can a relative-scale reading on plasterboard not be compared with one on concrete?
options: Concrete never holds water
A relative number only compares readings of the same material on the same meter
Relative scales are only for timber
Plasterboard readings are always in %MC
questions.explanation: Relative scales are not moisture content; they are comparable only within one material on one meter, which is why the reference must match the material.

questions.questionText: A 1.20 kg timber offcut reads 24 %MC; its reference is 11 %MC. About how much water must it lose?
options: About 0.156 kg (156 mL)
About 0.288 kg (288 mL)
About 0.013 kg (13 mL)
About 0.126 kg (126 mL)

questions.questionText: Why are reference readings taken before any equipment is switched on?
options: Airflow and dehumidification change the readings you are trying to capture
Meters do not work once equipment is running
Equipment trips the RCD while you take readings
Reference readings are only needed on the last day
questions.explanation: References describe the house at rest. Running air movers and dehumidifiers changes the materials and the air, so take references first.

quizzes.title: CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner — Module 2 check

questions.questionText: Which number shows that water has actually left the air?
options: A falling relative humidity on its own
A rising air temperature
A falling humidity ratio in g/kg
A louder dehumidifier
questions.explanation: Relative humidity depends on temperature, so warming the air lowers RH without removing water. The humidity ratio in g/kg changes only when water is added or removed.

questions.questionText: What is the dew point?
options: The temperature of a wet surface
The RH at which mould grows
The highest temperature on a drying job
The temperature to which air must be cooled for dew to form
questions.explanation: The Bureau of Meteorology defines dew point as the temperature to which air must be cooled, at constant pressure, for dew to occur.

questions.questionText: Day one reads 20 °C and 80 %RH (11.7 g/kg); day two reads 26 °C and 55 %RH (11.6 g/kg). What happened?
options: About a third of the water was removed
The room got much wetter
Almost no water was removed; the room warmed
The dehumidifier doubled its output
questions.explanation: The g/kg is almost unchanged, so the air holds the same water. The RH fell only because the temperature rose.

questions.questionText: Dehumidifier inlet reads 11.6 g/kg and outlet 7.9 g/kg. What is the g/kg depression?
options: 3.7 g/kg
1.5 g/kg
7.9 g/kg
questions.explanation: Depression is inlet minus outlet: 11.6 - 7.9 = 3.7 g/kg. Outlet below inlet shows the unit is removing water.

questions.questionText: The affected room reads 11.6 g/kg and an unaffected room 8.2 g/kg. What does this tell you?
options: Wet materials are still evaporating water into the affected room
The job is finished
The outside air is the problem
The dehumidifier has failed
questions.explanation: Affected above unaffected means evaporation is still loading the air. As drying proceeds the affected g/kg should trend down towards the unaffected reading.

questions.questionText: The room is 24 °C and 60 %RH (dew point 15.8 °C). The slab measures 14 °C. What is the risk?
options: No risk, because the slab is warmer than 10 °C
The slab will dry faster than the walls
Condensation on the slab, because it is below the dew point
The RH reading is wrong
questions.explanation: Air cooled to its dew point condenses. A surface colder than the room dew point can collect condensation, so lower the g/kg or warm the surface.

questions.questionText: How many grains per pound is 1 g/kg?
options: 7 grains per pound
70 grains per pound
0.7 grains per pound
7000 grains per pound
questions.explanation: There are 7000 grains in a pound, so 1 g per 1000 g of air is 7 grains per pound. Convert imported figures to g/kg before you log them.

quizzes.title: CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner — Module 3 check

questions.questionText: Which three things drive evaporation from a wet surface?
options: Light, noise and time
Pressure washing, chemicals and heat lamps
Only air movement
A vapour pressure difference, air movement at the surface, and energy
questions.explanation: Vapour moves from high to low vapour pressure, moving air thins the still layer at the surface, and evaporation needs energy (about 2.45 MJ per kg).

questions.questionText: Why does a wet slab under a floating floor dry slowly?
options: Concrete cannot hold water
It is dense and covered, so water must travel to a surface that airflow cannot reach
Floating floors are waterproof
Air movers do not work on concrete
questions.explanation: Dense materials hold water deep inside, and a covering blocks evaporation. The covering usually has to be lifted before the slab can dry.

questions.questionText: About how much heat is needed just to evaporate 10 L of water?
options: About 2.45 MJ (0.68 kWh)
About 24.5 MJ (6.8 kWh)
About 245 MJ (68 kWh)
About 0.25 MJ (0.07 kWh)
questions.explanation: 10 L is 10 kg; 10 x 2.45 MJ/kg = 24.5 MJ; divided by 3.6 MJ per kWh is about 6.8 kWh.

questions.questionText: Four air movers point at the centre of a room; the wet wall bases are not drying. What is the fix?
options: Add four more air movers in the centre
Turn the dehumidifier off
Open every window regardless of the weather
Angle the air movers along the wet wall bases so airflow sweeps the wet surfaces
questions.explanation: Airflow has to be on the wet surfaces. Angling along the wall bases, working around the room in one direction, puts the air where the water is.

questions.questionText: An imported air mover is rated at 2,000 CFM. What is that in metric?
options: About 3,400 m³/h
About 1,180 m³/h
About 34,000 m³/h
About 340 m³/h

questions.questionText: Visible mould is found on a wet wall. What happens to the air movers?
options: Run them at full speed to dry the mould
Point them at the mould from further away
Hold them: dry with dehumidifiers and air filtration under containment until remediation
Run them only overnight
questions.explanation: High airflow across mouldy surfaces spreads spores. Hold air movers until remediation, and treat suspected mould as mould.

questions.questionText: A wet wall reads colder than the air around it. Why?
options: The meter is broken
Cold walls cannot be wet
Air movers chill the wall by blowing cold air from outside
Evaporation draws heat from the surface
questions.explanation: Evaporating water takes heat from the air and the material, so a wet surface cools. It is also why heat speeds drying.

quizzes.title: CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner — Module 4 check

questions.questionText: How does a refrigerant dehumidifier remove water?
options: It filters water out with a paper filter
It heats water until it boils away
It cools air below its dew point on a cold coil so the water condenses and drains
It absorbs water into a turning wheel
questions.explanation: Air passes over a coil colder than its dew point; vapour condenses and drains, and the air is reheated before it leaves.

questions.questionText: Why does a refrigerant unit remove little water in a cold Dunedin basement?
options: Refrigerant units only work outdoors
The coil must run close to freezing to get below the dew point, and it can ice
Cold air holds more water than warm air
The unit needs outside air to work
questions.explanation: At 12 °C and 85 %RH the dew point is 9.6 °C. The coil must run below that, close to freezing, so icing and low output are likely.

questions.questionText: Which dehumidifier type keeps working best when the air is cold?
options: A desiccant dehumidifier
A conventional refrigerant dehumidifier
An air mover
An air filtration device
questions.explanation: Desiccants adsorb water rather than condensing it on a cold coil, so they keep working in cold, dry conditions.

questions.questionText: What must be done with a desiccant dehumidifier’s reactivation air?
options: Blow it back into the wet room
Run it through an air mover
Duct it out of the drying zone, usually outside
Nothing; it is dry air
questions.explanation: Reactivation air carries the removed water as warm, wet air. Returning it to the room would put the water straight back.

questions.questionText: Process airflow 340 m³/h, depression 3.7 g/kg. About how much water is removed per day?
options: About 36 L/day
About 3.6 L/day
About 360 L/day
About 1.5 L/day

questions.questionText: The calculated removal is 36 L/day but the pump log shows 10 L/day. What should you check?
options: Nothing; calculations always overestimate
Add more air movers
Switch the dehumidifier off
Filter, outlet, pump line and meter: a large mismatch points to a fault or misreading
questions.explanation: The calculation and the condensate log should broadly agree. A big gap points to a blocked filter, restricted outlet, leaking pump line or a misread meter.

questions.questionText: A desiccant’s reactivation duct has been left venting into the drying zone. What happens?
options: The desiccant dries faster
The removed water goes straight back into the room air
Nothing; reactivation air is dry
The unit switches to refrigerant mode
questions.explanation: Reactivation air carries the water the wheel collected as warm, wet air. Vent it out of the drying zone, usually outside.

quizzes.title: CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner — Module 5 check

questions.questionText: Inside reads 11.6 g/kg. Outside in Townsville reads 19.0 g/kg. Should you open the windows to dry?
options: Yes; any fresh air helps
No; outside air is wetter, so keep the zone closed
Yes, because it is warm outside
Only if the RH outside is under 90 %
questions.explanation: Open drying helps only when outside g/kg is lower than inside. Townsville summer air is far wetter, so stay closed and dehumidify.

questions.questionText: Christchurch outside air is 6.4 g/kg at 9 °C; inside is 8.4 g/kg at 18 °C. Why may opening up still slow drying?
options: The outside air is wetter
Cold air carries more water
Opening windows trips the RCD
The cold air chills the materials, so evaporation slows
questions.explanation: Outside air is drier, but at 9 °C it removes heat that evaporation needs. Closed drying with electric heat is usually the better plan.

questions.questionText: What is the rule for fuel-burning heaters and generators on a drying job?
options: Never run them indoors: they produce carbon monoxide
Run them indoors only with a window open a little
Run them indoors overnight when nobody is home
Use them in an internal garage only
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide has no colour, smell or taste and can kill. Australian and New Zealand guidance says never to run them inside or in poorly ventilated areas.

questions.questionText: About how much power can one 10 A circuit supply at 230 V?
options: About 1150 W
About 23,000 W
About 2300 W
About 230 W
questions.explanation: 230 V x 10 A = 2300 W in total, and several GPOs often share one circuit.

questions.questionText: A dehumidifier (4.5 A), four air movers (1.2 A each) and an air filtration device (2.0 A) share one 10 A circuit. What is the total and what do you do?
options: 7.7 A: fine as it is
9.3 A: fine with no headroom needed
6.9 A: add more equipment
11.3 A: over the rating, so split the load across circuits
questions.explanation: 4.5 + 4.8 + 2.0 = 11.3 A, over 10 A before any start-up surge. Split it, for example 6.9 A and 4.4 A on separate circuits.

questions.questionText: How do Australian and New Zealand rules on testing and tagging differ?
options: They are identical in every respect
New Zealand bans testing and tagging
Australia requires inspection and testing of equipment in hostile conditions; New Zealand requires safe equipment and treats tagging as one way to show it
Australia has no rules on electrical equipment
questions.explanation: In Australia, equipment in hostile conditions is regularly inspected and tested by a competent person. WorkSafe NZ says tagging is not mandatory but equipment must be safe and RCD-protected in damp conditions.

questions.questionText: Where must a generator be placed on a drying job?
options: In the internal garage with the door half open
Outside, away from openings, never indoors or in an internal garage
In the wet room, so its heat helps drying
Anywhere, if a window is open
questions.explanation: Generators produce carbon monoxide. Both Queensland and New Zealand guidance say never to run one indoors, including an internal garage.

quizzes.title: CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner — Module 6 check

questions.questionText: Air g/kg is rising and the house feels sticky after more air movers were added. What is the likely cause?
options: Evaporation is outrunning dehumidification
The materials are already dry
The RCD is faulty
The outside air is too dry
questions.explanation: More airflow lifted more water than the dehumidifiers could remove. Check the depression and add dehumidification or reduce airflow.

questions.questionText: The air is dry but a timber floor has not moved for a day. What is a sound single change?
options: Add air movers across the whole house
Declare it dry
Focus heat and airflow on that floor, or open it up, and record why
Turn off the dehumidifier
questions.explanation: Dry air with a static material means the water is bound deep or covered. Change one thing aimed at that material and record the reason.

questions.questionText: Which item is essential in the drying file?
options: Final readings showing each material at its dry standard
The brand of the technician’s van
A guess of how long it took
The owner’s opinion that it feels dry
questions.explanation: The file proves the outcome: references, daily logs, changes with reasons, photos and final readings at the dry standard.

questions.questionText: In the Christchurch case, what is done before any ceiling lining is cut?
options: Cut a test hole to look inside
Spray the lining with antimicrobial
Nothing; weatherboard houses have no asbestos
Arrange asbestos sampling, because the house was built before 2000
questions.explanation: A 1978 house may contain asbestos in textured ceilings and older linings. Sample first and treat suspect material as asbestos until results return.

questions.questionText: Why is closed drying with heat and a desiccant chosen in the Christchurch case?
options: Desiccants are always cheaper
The air is cold, so a refrigerant coil would run near freezing and outside air would chill the house
Refrigerant units are banned in New Zealand
The owner asked for it
questions.explanation: At 12 °C the refrigerant coil would ice. Heat drives evaporation, and a desiccant keeps removing water in cold conditions.

questions.questionText: A A$2,400 ex-GST drying charge is invoiced in Australia. What is the price including GST?
questions.explanation: GST is 10 % in Australia: 2,400 x 1.10 = A$2,640.

questions.questionText: A job is declared dry because the air reads 6.5 g/kg, but a slab is still above its reference. Is it finished?
options: Yes; dry air means dry materials
Yes, if the owner agrees
Only if the dehumidifier is still running
No; every mapped material must reach its dry standard
questions.explanation: Dry air is not the finish line. The file must show every mapped point at its reference reading before the job is verified dry.

quizzes.title: CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner — Final designation exam

questions.questionText: What is the drying goal for each wet material?
options: To return it to its dry standard, measured against the same material unaffected
To make its surface feel dry to the touch
To get the meter reading to zero
To dry it for exactly three days
questions.explanation: The goal is a measured return to the dry standard, set from an unaffected reference of the same material, same meter and same scale.

questions.questionText: In New Zealand, which Act places the primary duty of care on the PCBU?
options: The Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004
The Consumer Guarantees Act 1993
The Health and Safety at Work Act 2015
The Electricity (Safety) Regulations 2010
questions.explanation: Section 36 of the HSWA 2015 sets the PCBU’s primary duty. Victoria’s OHS Act 2004 is an Australian state law.

questions.questionText: In Australia, a licence is needed to remove how much non-friable asbestos?
options: More than 1 m²
More than 50 m²
Any amount, in every state
More than 10 m²
questions.explanation: A Class B licence is needed above 10 m² of non-friable asbestos, and the ACT does not allow homeowners or tradespeople to remove any amount themselves.

questions.questionText: Why log g/kg rather than relative humidity alone?
options: g/kg is easier to read on a meter
Relative humidity is an imperial unit
g/kg does not change when air warms or cools, so it shows real water removal
g/kg is only used outside
questions.explanation: RH depends on temperature. The humidity ratio changes only when water is added or removed, so it is the number to compare.

questions.questionText: Which five points are read on every visit?
options: Only the affected room
Outside, unaffected room, affected room, dehumidifier inlet and outlet
The switchboard, the van, the meter, the owner and the insurer
Five random places in the wet room
questions.explanation: Those five readings show the context, the target, the evaporation load and the dehumidifier’s performance.

questions.questionText: The dehumidifier outlet reads higher in g/kg than its inlet. What does that mean?
options: The unit is not removing water: investigate it
The unit is working very well
The room is fully dry
Nothing; outlet readings are not useful
questions.explanation: A working dehumidifier’s outlet is drier than its inlet. A higher outlet g/kg means a fault, a misreading, or reactivation air getting back in.

questions.questionText: A cold external wall is at 13 °C and the room dew point is 16.3 °C. What do you do?
options: Ignore it; walls cannot condense
Add air movers aimed at the wall from outside
Lower the room g/kg, warm the surface, or both, before trusting readings there
Open the windows in a humid coastal summer
questions.explanation: A surface below the dew point can collect condensation, which would mask true drying. Fix the condition first.

questions.questionText: What does an air mover do?
options: Moves air across wet surfaces to thin the still layer and carry vapour away
Removes water from the air
Heats the room
Filters mould spores
questions.explanation: Air movers drive evaporation. Dehumidifiers remove the water from the air, and air filtration devices capture particles.

questions.questionText: Why might more air movers make a job worse?
options: They cool the dehumidifier coil
They always trip RCDs
They make the materials denser
They can lift more water into the air than the dehumidifiers remove
questions.explanation: Airflow and dehumidification must be in step. Without enough dehumidification the room g/kg rises and drying stalls.

questions.questionText: A desiccant unit moves 500 m³/h and lowers air from 7.4 to 3.0 g/kg. About how much water per day?
options: About 6.3 L/day
About 63 L/day
About 630 L/day
About 26 L/day

questions.questionText: The daily litres from a dehumidifier fall steadily as the job proceeds. What is the usual reason?
options: The unit is broken
The room is drying, so inlet g/kg and the depression fall
The supply frequency has changed
The filter has been removed
questions.explanation: A falling daily figure is expected as the air dries, provided the materials are also approaching their dry standard.

questions.questionText: When does open drying with outside air help?
options: Whenever it is not raining
Only at night
Whenever outside RH is below 100 %
When outside g/kg is lower than inside and the air is warm enough not to chill the materials
questions.explanation: Both conditions matter: drier air by g/kg and a temperature that does not slow evaporation.

questions.questionText: Which heat source is acceptable inside a drying zone?
options: Electric heat on a budgeted, RCD-protected circuit
An LPG cabinet heater
A petrol generator running a heater
A kerosene space heater
questions.explanation: Fuel-burning heaters and engines produce carbon monoxide. Only electric heat goes inside, within the power budget.

questions.questionText: What is the nominal mains supply in both Australia and New Zealand?
options: 200 V at 60 Hz
240 V at 60 Hz
230 V at 50 Hz
400 V at 50 Hz for every GPO
questions.explanation: Both countries supply a nominal 230 V at 50 Hz to standard outlets. Three-phase 400 V is not the standard GPO supply.

questions.questionText: A larger desiccant has a 15 A plug. What is the right response?
options: File the earth pin to fit a 10 A GPO
Use any adaptor from the van
Plug it into a power board with other machines
Use a 15 A outlet or a suitable supply; never modify the plug or force an adaptor
questions.explanation: A 15 A plug is made not to fit a 10 A outlet. It needs a supply rated for it.

questions.questionText: On a damp New Zealand job, what does the Electricity (Safety) Regulations 2010 regime expect of leads and appliances?
options: Nothing until they have been tagged
Testing every hour
RCD protection in damp conditions, and equipment kept electrically safe
Use of battery tools only
questions.explanation: WorkSafe NZ says equipment must be RCD-protected in circumstances such as damp conditions and be electrically safe; tagging is one way to show it.

questions.questionText: What trip current applies to an Australian workplace RCD on a socket outlet up to 20 A?
options: No more than 300 mA
No more than 30 mA
No more than 3 A
No more than 10 A
questions.explanation: WorkSafe ACT guidance sets a tripping current not exceeding 30 mA for socket outlets not exceeding 20 A.

questions.questionText: A drying log shows a stall. What is the disciplined response?
options: Diagnose from the readings, change one thing, and record why
Change everything at once
Stop taking readings
Wait a week without changes
questions.explanation: Changing one thing at a time, with the reason recorded, lets the next reading show whether the change worked.

questions.questionText: What is the New Zealand consumer guarantee for services such as drying?
options: Services are always free if late
There is no guarantee for services
Services are carried out with reasonable care and skill
Only goods carry guarantees
questions.explanation: Section 28 of the Consumer Guarantees Act 1993 guarantees that services are carried out with reasonable care and skill.

questions.questionText: Which two pieces of evidence earn the CARSI Structural Drying Practitioner designation?
options: The graded practical task and the final designation exam
Attendance and a photo of the van
A supplier invoice and a meter receipt
A first-aid certificate and a CARSI login
questions.explanation: The designation is awarded on the practical task, graded against the rubric, and the final designation exam.
